claim: Imported merchandise is appraised on the basis, and in the order, of the listed valuation methods, starting with transaction value.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Imported merchandise will be appraised on the basis, and in the order, of the following:

claim: Transaction value is the price actually paid or payable for merchandise when sold for exportation to the United States, plus specified additions.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: when sold for exportation to the United States

claim: Price actually paid or payable means the total payment, direct or indirect, made by the buyer to or for the benefit of the seller.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: “Price actually paid or payable” means the total payment (whether direct or indirect

claim: Price actually paid or payable excludes charges for transportation, insurance and related services for the international shipment.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: exclusive of any charges, costs, or expenses incurred for transportation, insurance

claim: Packing costs incurred by the buyer are added to the price.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: The packing costs incurred by the buyer with respect to the imported merchandise;

claim: Any selling commission incurred by the buyer is added to the price.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Any selling commission incurred by the buyer with respect to the imported merchandise;

claim: The value of any assist, apportioned as appropriate, is added to the price.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: The value, apportioned as appropriate, of any assist;

claim: Any royalty or license fee related to the imported merchandise that the buyer is required to pay is added to the price.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Any royalty or license fee related to the imported merchandise that the buyer is required to pay

claim: Proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal, or use of the merchandise that accrue to the seller are added to the price.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: The proceeds of any subsequent resale, disposal, or use of the imported merchandise that accrue

claim: Additions are made only to the extent each amount is not otherwise included in the price actually paid or payable.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: to the extent that each amount is not otherwise included within the price actually paid or payable

claim: Additions must be based on sufficient information; otherwise transaction value is treated as one that cannot be determined.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: based on sufficient information

claim: A selling commission is any commission paid to the seller's agent who is related to or controlled by, or works for or on behalf of, the manufacturer or the seller.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: any commission paid to the seller's agent, who is related to or controlled by, or works for or on behalf of, the manufacturer or the seller.
verifier_note: 152.102(b) also covers an agent who 'works for or on behalf of' the manufacturer or seller; the claim omitted that limb. Claim, body sentence and common-mistakes row updated.

claim: Materials, components, parts and similar items incorporated in the imported merchandise are assists.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Materials, components, parts, and similar items incorporated in the imported merchandise.

claim: Tools, dies, molds and similar items used to produce the imported merchandise are assists.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Tools, dies, molds, and similar items used in the production of the imported merchandise.

claim: Engineering, development, artwork, design work, and plans and sketches necessary for production are assists.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Engineering, development, artwork, design work, and plans and sketches

claim: Engineering and design work counts as an assist only when undertaken elsewhere than in the United States.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: undertaken elsewhere than in the United States

claim: For an assist acquired from an unrelated seller, its value is the cost of its acquisition.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: the value of the assist is the cost of its acquisition

claim: For an assist produced by the buyer or a related person, its value is the cost of its production.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: its value would be the cost of its production

claim: Whether a royalty is dutiable turns on whether the buyer must pay it as a condition of sale of the merchandise for exportation to the United States.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: as a condition of sale of the merchandise for exportation to the United States

claim: Royalties or license fees for patents covering processes to manufacture the imported merchandise are generally dutiable.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: Royalties or license fees for patents covering processes to manufacture the imported merchandise

claim: CBP will not disregard a transaction value solely because the buyer and seller are related.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: The Center director shall not disregard a transaction value solely because the buyer and seller are related.

claim: Transaction value applies if the buyer and seller are not related, or are related but the transaction value is acceptable.
publisher: eCFR — Office of the Federal Register
evidence: The buyer and seller are not related, or the buyer and seller are related but the transaction value is acceptable.

claim: CBP's current interpretation, as described in 2008, is to base transaction value on the price paid by the buyer in the first or earlier sale.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: CBP's current interpretation is to base transaction value on the price paid by the buyer in the first or earlier sale

claim: That treatment requires the importer to establish by sufficient evidence that the earlier sale was an arm's length sale.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: provided the importer can establish by sufficient evidence that this was an arm's length sale

claim: It also requires that, at the time of the earlier sale, the merchandise was clearly destined for exportation to the United States.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: and that, at the time of such sale, the merchandise was clearly destined for exportation to the United States

claim: CBP's notice describes the Nissho Iwai test: the sale must be an arm's length sale and the goods must be clearly destined for export to the U.S.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: The sale must be an arm's length sale and the goods must be clearly destined for export to the U.S.

claim: In Synergy, as described by CBP, garments were found clearly destined for export by virtue of their labels.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: by virtue of the labels

claim: CBP noted that an intermediary often sells the same merchandise to buyers in the U.S. and in other countries.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: the intermediary often sells the same merchandise both to buyers in the U.S. and to buyers in other countries

claim: CBP stated that the importer's burden increases greatly when it declares a transaction value based on the first sale.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: The importer's burden increases greatly when an importer declares a transaction value based on the first sale

claim: CBP's notice cites T.D. 96-87 as part of its existing first-sale guidance.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
evidence: See T.D. 96-87, vols. 30/31 Cust. B. & Dec. Nos. 52/1 (January 2, 1997)

claim: CBP's 2008 proposal would have typically based transaction value on the price paid in the last sale occurring before the goods were introduced into the United States.
publisher: Federal Register — U.S. Customs and Border Protection
